## R Markdown

This is an R Markdown document. Markdown is a simple formatting syntax for authoring HTML, PDF, and MS Word documents. For more details on using R Markdown see <http://rmarkdown.rstudio.com>.

When you click the **Knit** button a document will be generated that includes both content as well as the output of any embedded R code chunks within the document. You can embed an R code chunk like this:

```{r cars}
summary(cars)
```

## Including Plots

You can also embed plots, for example:

```{r pressure, echo=FALSE}
plot(pressure)
```

Note that the `echo = FALSE` parameter was added to the code chunk to prevent printing of the R code that generated the plot.

## Read in the auto-mpg.csv data set into your new R markdown file 

I would use r to read the auto mpg file and assign it to a data frame called data

```{r}
  data <- read.csv("auto-mpg.csv")
```

## Explore the data (using summary statistics and plots) and check which columns from the continous variables look normally distributed.

```{r}
  str(data)
```
So from the output above, we can see that there are 398 observations of 9 variables. Out of the 9 variables, 7 are continous/numerical variables while two are categorical variables. 

# I would now explore the continous/numerical variables to see which looks normally distributed.

# I would be examining the MPG variable for its distribution
```{r}
  hist(data$mpg, main = "Histogram of MPG", xlab = "MPG", ylab = "Frequency", col = "blue")
```
This (MPG) leans towards right-skewed distribution.

# I would be examining the Cylinders variable for its distribution
```{r}
  hist(data$cylinders, main = "Histogram of Cylinders", xlab = "Cylinders", ylab = "Frequency", col = "navy")
```
This (cylinders) is not a normally distributed histogram.

# I would be examining the Displacement variable for its distribution
```{r}
  hist(data$displacement, main = "Histogram of Displacement", xlab = "Displacement", ylab = "Frequency", col = "lightblue")
```
This (Displacement) is not a normal distribution histogram.

# I would be examining the Weight variable for its distribution
```{r}
  hist(data$weight, main = "Histogram of Weight", xlab = "Weight", ylab = "Frequency", col = "red")
```
This (Weight) is a right skewed distribution histogram.

# I would be examining the Acceleration variable for its distribution
```{r}
  hist(data$acceleration, main = "Histogram of Acceleration", xlab = "Acceleration", ylab = "Frequency", col = "green")
```
The Acceleration histogram is a normal distribution histogram.

# I would be examining the Model.Year variable for its distribution
```{r}
  hist(data$model.year, main = "Histogram of Model Year", xlab = "Model Year", ylab = "Frequency", col = "yellow")
```
Model.year is not normally distributed.

# I would be examining the Origin variable for its distribution
```{r}
  hist(data$origin, main = "Histogram of Origin", xlab = "Origin", ylab = "Frequency", col = "cyan")
```
The origin variable is not normally distributed.

# I would now explore the categorical variables using boxplot

# I would be examining the horsepower variable for its distribution
```{r}
  boxplot(table(data$horsepower), main = "Boxplot of Horsepower", xlab = "Horsepower", ylab = "Frequency", col = "violet")
```
I can't comment on the distribution of this.

# I would be examining the Car name variable for its distribution
```{r}
  boxplot(table(data$car.name), main = "Boxplot of Car Name", xlab = "Car Name", ylab = "Frequency", col = "lightblue")
```
This is not normally distributed.

## Compute a 95% confidence interval for the mean for one of the variable that appears to be normally distributed.
```{r}
  t.test(data$acceleration, conf.level = 0.95)
```

Acceleration appears to be normally distributed and I have computed the confidence interval for it. The 95% confidence interval for acceleration is 15.296 to 15.840, rounded to three decimal places.

## The model years range from the 70s and the 80s. What proportion of cars are from the 80s?
```{r}
   mean(data$model.year >= 80) * 100
```
Approximately 22.4% of cars are from the 80s

## Compute a 90% confidence interval for the proportion of cars from the 80s?
```{r}
  prop.test(sum(data$model.year >= 80), nrow(data), conf.level = 0.9)
```
The 90% confidence interval for the proportion of cars from the 80s is between 0.19 and 0.26 rounded to two decimal place.

## Change the confidence level and track what happens to the width of the confidence interval for 6. and 8.
```{r}
  prop.test(sum(data$model.year >= 80), nrow(data), conf.level = 0.6)
```
```{r}
  prop.test(sum(data$model.year >= 80), nrow(data), conf.level = 0.8)
```
The width gets narrower as the confidence level reduces.
